planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; keep the crown just at soil level and mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native forest floor.

directions: Broad buckler fern is a robust, deciduous woodland fern native to cool, moist forests across Europe and also found in the Pacific Northwest of North America, forming a broad, shuttlecock-like clump of dark green, triangular, finely divided fronds carried on stipes marked with near-black, shaggy scales at the base. It thrives in deep shade and consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, tolerating boggier conditions than many Dryopteris and performing especially well along shaded stream banks and in cool ravine gardens. Larger and coarser in texture than the related D. carthusiana and D. expansa, it makes an excellent bold-textured backdrop fern for woodland borders. Divide congested clumps in early spring, keeping several fronds and roots per division.

planting.note: Tuck small divisions into gritty, humus-poor soil in rock crevices or a cool scree bed in partial shade; this arctic-alpine fern resents rich garden soil and overwatering.

directions: Alpine cliff fern is a diminutive, circumboreal rock fern found in cool, mossy crevices on cliffs and talus slopes from Greenland, Labrador, and Quebec across to Scandinavia and the mountains of Britain, forming small tufts of narrow, once- to twice-pinnate fronds only a few inches tall. It demands sharp drainage, cool root conditions, and a lean, gritty substrate, declining quickly in rich, wet garden soil or summer heat and humidity. Best suited to a shaded crevice or trough in a cool rock garden rather than an ordinary shade border, where it can be grown alongside other alpine specialties. It is slow-growing and best left undisturbed once established, dividing only when a clump has filled its crevice.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in humus-rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial to full shade; this Pacific Northwest mountain native is adapted to the duff layer of conifer forests and resents heavy, waterlogged soils.

directions: Idaho barren strawberry is a low, evergreen native groundcover of coniferous forest understories in the northern Rocky Mountains and interior Pacific Northwest, forming a slowly spreading mat of glossy, three-lobed, strawberry-like leaves. Small five-petaled yellow flowers appear in a brief spring display just above the foliage, followed by inconspicuous dry fruit rather than edible berries. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to knit into a tidy, weed-suppressing carpet beneath pines, firs, and other conifers, tolerating dry summer shade once established better than many woodland groundcovers. Use it at the front of a shaded native bed or beneath open conifer canopy where a fine-textured, low-maintenance evergreen mat is wanted.

planting.note: Plant divisions into gritty, humus-rich soil tucked against rock or in canyon-bottom shade; keep consistently moist during the growing season but allow the fern to go summer-dormant if conditions turn dry.

directions: Southwestern brittle fern grows naturally along shaded, seasonally moist canyon walls and rocky stream banks across Arizona, New Mexico, and the Trans-Pecos region of Texas south into Mexico, forming small clumps of delicate, lacy, twice-pinnate fronds on brittle stipes. It is deciduous, dying back readily when summer heat and dryness set in and re-emerging with cooler, wetter conditions in fall or spring, much like other Cystopteris species. In the garden it wants a shaded crevice or canyon-style rock garden setting with gritty but moisture-retentive soil, making it a good choice for Southwestern native plant collections where few other ferns tolerate the region's heat and alkalinity. Combine with columbine and native sedges in a shaded dry-stream or rock garden planting.

planting.note: Transplant divisions or plugs into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade; weak trailing stems root at the nodes, so space plants loosely and let them fill in.

directions: Roundleaf bedstraw is a low, sprawling native groundcover of rich, shaded deciduous woods in the Appalachian and southeastern uplands, distinguished from its relatives by broadly rounded, almost circular leaves arranged in whorls along weak, square stems. It spreads by rooting stem tips into a loose, open mat rather than forming a dense turf, making it best used as a textural filler threading between larger woodland perennials rather than as solid-coverage groundcover. Tiny greenish-white flowers appear in open clusters in early summer, followed by small bristly fruit. It is an unassuming but genuinely shade-tolerant native filler for naturalized woodland plantings, easiest to source from native plant specialty growers.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; give it room to spread since it roots along its runners wherever they touch soil.

directions: Chinese meehania is a stoloniferous woodland groundcover from central China, grown mainly by shade-garden specialists as a less commonly offered relative of the Korean and American Meehania species already in cultivation. It forms a low mat of scalloped, semi-evergreen leaves and sends up short spikes of tubular, blue-violet flowers in spring, drawing early pollinators to the woodland floor. It spreads by surface stolons that root at the nodes, filling in gaps beneath trees and shrubs at a manageable pace that is easily curtailed by trimming stray runners. Less reliably winter-hardy than American Meehania cordata, it performs best in warm-temperate shade gardens with reliably moist, humus-rich soil.
